definition: For each funding settlement T of a perpetual paying F_T: dprem = prem(T+5m) - prem(T-5m), prem = perp/index - 1; pass-through beta = E[sign(F) dprem] / E[|F|]. mechanism: A perpetual is a zero-cost contract that pays a lump cash flow F_T at known times. definition: At a snapshot of Hyperliquid's largest accounts, L is the notional of long positions whose liquidation price lies 1-5% below the mark and S the notional of shorts liquidated 1-5% above it. When one side holds at least 75% of L + S and L + S is at least 1% of the coin's open interest, enter toward that side at the next minute, take profit at its notional-weighted mean distance D, stop at D on the other side (a minute reaching both is a stop), or leave after 48 hours; one position per coin; judged on Binance spot one-minute bars after 0.1% a side.
disappears_when: Clusters are small against the depth of the venues that set the mark (bitcoin's books on Binance and Coinbase dwarf most Hyperliquid clusters), the oracle-anchored mark resists pushing Hyperliquid's own book, or traders move to isolated, low-leverage or opaque positions.
holding_and_risk: Minutes to 48 hours. Risk: the price moves the other way to the stop, gaps through both levels in fast markets, clusters migrate as positions are opened and closed, and followers crowd the move.
mechanism: Liquidations are forced, price-insensitive orders whose only trigger is the price. When forced trades are predictable in size and trigger, it pays others to trade ahead of them in the same direction, push the price to the trigger and supply the liquidity the forced trades then demand (Brunnermeier & Pedersen 2005, predatory trading); a triggered cluster adds its own forced flow, which carries the price on (a cascade). Hyperliquid makes the triggers public: both effects predict the price reaches a large visible cluster before an equally distant level with none.

return_relation: With symmetric target and stop at D, the expected net per trade is (2p - 1) x D - 2c, where p is the probability the cluster side is reached first; a driftless price gives p = 0.5. The effect should grow with the cluster's share of open interest, its lopsidedness and its closeness.
why_exists: Hyperliquid keeps accounts and positions on its own chain, so every position's liquidation price can be read by anyone; nowhere else is the location of forced orders public. Pushing the price costs the push's impact; the reward is the forced flow's impact and fills against it at better prices.
why_not_competed_away: Competition among predators is what would produce the effect: the more of them, the more reliably the price is pushed to clusters; the effect then lives in the price path, and a slow follower entering at a half-hourly snapshot pays only the move. It goes away only if hunting stops paying (clusters too small against global depth) or traders stop leaving their liquidation prices where others can see them.

mechanism: A rise led by leveraged buyers shows as a perpetual premium; their demand is borrowed and comes back out when the positions close (this record's SQZ-1, BAS-1 and CASC-1 found coins under leverage stress do worse than the market for days to weeks). A rise led by spot buyers is paid in full and owes nothing: it reflects new holders, does not have to be unwound, and the slower holders it attracts carry it further.

name: MSTR-1 Strategy's weekly bitcoin purchases as a dated buyer
reason: Known, contradicted, and not unseen. Strategy (MicroStrategy) buys bitcoin with the proceeds of its share sales and announces each week's buying the next Monday, so a long bitcoin CFD in the weeks after an announcement would front-run a dated buyer. TD Cowen found its purchases had minimal, statistically weak effect on the price; K33 found bitcoin tends to dip after announcements of more than 1,000 BTC and recover within days; the larger flow multipliers (2% to 6% per $1 billion, Sygnum and Deribit) come from regressions of flows that chase prices (all search results, news coverage of the studies). Power: about 90 announcements, a 3-day standard deviation near 5%, so t 3.0 needs +1.6% over three days, more than a dip that reverses; the weekly version needs a 3% difference between weeks at bitcoin's 9% weekly volatility. And bitcoin's path in 2020-2026, with Strategy's buying, is in the designer's training data, so only a forward stage would be unseen, and at these volatilities no forward stage of a year or two can reach t 3.0.

name: SGC-1 the Hong Kong index while Southbound Stock Connect is shut for mainland holidays
reason: Power. Southbound trading runs only when both markets are open, so on mainland holidays the largest net buyer of Hong Kong shares (20% to 30% of the turnover, record net buying of about HK$808 billion in 2024 and HK$1.4 trillion in 2025) is absent while Hong Kong trades; an HK50 CFD bought at the close before it reopens (or sold short during the closure, stated) would collect the gap. No study was found; the news is mixed (the Hang Seng fell 2.6% on 2025-10-02 with the link shut, was flat over that Golden Week, and rose after some reopenings), and the flow turned to net selling in 2026 (search results only). The net buying is about 0.01% of Hong Kong's market value a day: even five times that for an inelastic market, a four-day closure moves the index about 0.2%. Since the flow grew large (2020) there are about 35 closures; at a standard deviation near 3.5% over one, t 3.0 needs about +1.8% each, nine times the plausible size.

name: TQB-1 bitcoin at the quarter-ends when Tether books its profit allocation to bitcoin

About 100 days of large moves since 2024, at a standard deviation near 0.8% over that hour, need about 24 bp for t 3.0, and a CFD's round trip of 3 to 6 bp takes part of what is there. Checked on 2026-11-24 (search results only): the trade press describes, week after week, the Monday gap following the weekend's GFS and European model changes, warmer guidance down and colder up: the market prices the change at the open, and the reversals it mentions during the week are anecdotes, not a pattern; no study of a systematic under- or over-reaction was found. The forecasts the market trades on (gas-weighted degree days) are a paid product; free archives (the CPC outlooks, the raw GFS runs) would have to be weighted by hand. Natural gas's daily history is read by the lab's EIA panel, so only a forward stage would be unseen, at about 50 weekends a year against a Monday gap with a standard deviation near 3%.

name: AMM-1 concentrated-liquidity range exits
reason: Too small for t 3.0 and for the costs, by its own arithmetic. Round 2 kept AMM-1 waiting for a node or a keyed indexer. Checked on 2026-11-24 (search results only): price discovery for ether happens on the centralized venues (arXiv 2506.08718; arXiv 2112.07386); large Uniswap v3 providers adjust out-of-range positions in response to informed flow (arXiv 2307.13772); a 2026 working paper finds their orders carry some price impact of their own (Klein and others); none measures a re-centring flow that predicts ether's next move. Power: since May 2021 ether has had roughly 100 to 150 days up more than 5% (an estimate from its volatility; a long-only rule) and about twice as many with short sales on a CFD; with a next-day standard deviation near 4.5%, t 3.0 needs about 1.2% a trade long only, about 0.9% with short sales. A generous upper bound on the re-centring buy after such a day, about $90 million against roughly $20 billion of ether traded a day (estimates; the search found only market-wide totals: decentralized spot volume about $131 billion in July 2026, 24% of the centralized venues'), gives an impact near 0.25% by the square-root law, and automated managers re-centre within the hours of the move itself. The cost gate asks three times a 0.2% round trip, 0.6%. Ether's daily history is read by the lab, so only a forward stage would be unseen.

name: CHL-1 China's price limits and Hong Kong the next day
reason: Too few events at the tradable level, for a mechanism the evidence says has weakened. Round 2 kept CHL-1 waiting for daily limit hits per stock. Checked on 2026-11-24 (search results only): Li, Zheng and Chen (2014), comparing the A, H and N shares of the same firms, find price limits curb continuation but leave volatility spillover and trading interference; Lu (2016) finds those effects insignificant among high-activity stocks, the large names that dominate the Hang Seng; Chong and Kwok (a CUHK working paper) find Stock Connect alleviates the delayed price discovery limits cause; no study tests the H-share side the next day. Power: days of mass limit hits (the CSI 300 down 5% or more) number roughly 50 to 70 since 2007 and roughly 25 to 30 since Stock Connect began in November 2014 (estimates); with the Hang Seng's next-day standard deviation near 3% on such days, t 3.0 needs about 1.2% a trade over 60 days (1.6% over 30), while dual-listed names carry roughly a third of the index's weight (an estimate), diluting an overshoot of their H shares to a few tenths of a percent. The rule trades both directions, so it needs short sales on a CFD. The Hang Seng's daily history is read by the lab (scripts/rc_eq.py, scripts/div2.py, scripts/trnd2_probe.py), so only a forward stage would be unseen, at a handful of such days a year, or none.

name: DAT-1 crypto treasury companies below their coins' value as sellers of bitcoin and ether
reason: Small, disclosed after the sale, and too new to measure. A company holding bitcoin or ether whose shares trade below the value of its coins (an mNAV below 1) can no longer issue stock to buy, and buying back shares with coins is accretive, so it turns seller; debt repayment forces others. Checked on 2026-11-24 (search results only): in 2026 37 of the 100 largest bitcoin treasury companies traded below their holdings and Strategy's mNAV fell below 1 for the first time; the sales reported are tens of millions of dollars each (FG Nexus about 10,900 ETH, about $33 million; ETHZilla about $40 million; Sequans 314 BTC; Nakamoto about 600 BTC in June), and about $218 million by Strategy over the year; each is disclosed after it is done; commentary disputes any effect on the price, no study isolates one, and Strategy faces no near-term forced sale (Pepperstone). Power and costs: a $50 million sale against roughly $30 billion of bitcoin traded a day (an estimate) moves the price about 0.1% by the square-root law, a fifth of the cost gate's 0.6% on a 0.2% spot round trip. A predictable flow would need the regime itself as the signal, and the regime began in 2026: a handful of months, with bitcoin's and ether's daily history read by the lab, so only a forward stage of a few regime changes would be unseen. The rule would sell, so it needs short sales on a CFD.

name: GRL-1 energy CFDs in the commodity-index roll window (the Goldman roll)
reason: A known, dated flow whose price effect lives in the calendar spread, not in the price the owner can trade, and was found to reverse within minutes. Commodity index funds (the GSCI's roll, the 5th to 9th business days of each month) and oil ETFs sell the front month and buy the next on dated days. Checked on 2026-11-24 (search results only): Mou (2011, SSRN 1716841) finds the roll's impact significant and its front-running profitable to 2009 through the spread's narrowing; Bessembinder, Carrion, Tuttle and Venkataraman ('Liquidity, Resiliency and Market Quality Around Predictable Trades', JFE) find liquidity improves on roll dates and over 99% of the temporary impact reverses within ten minutes, with the ETFs paying about 30 bp to roll (data to 2011); a Two Sigma note (2017) doubts a lasting arbitrage; no study after 2011 was found. Power and costs: on the owner's instrument, a front-month oil CFD, the spread's effect is buried in the outright price's volatility, near 5% over the window, so about 170 windows from 2012 need about 1.2% a window for t 3.0. Trading the spread itself needs two expiring futures CFDs (if the broker offers them), a short sale, and four fills at about 0.16% in all (an estimate), so the cost gate asks about 0.5% against at most the 0.3% the ETFs paid before 2011.
